EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN ─ STOCK-MARKET RESPONSE TO MONETARY-POLICY SURPRISES  
Sample: All 131 FOMC announcement days, 1989-2002; daily CRSP returns (value-weighted market, 17 FF industries, and individual stocks); CBOT federal-funds-futures data.

-----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
-----------------------------------------------------------------
High-frequency event-study / instrumental-variables (HFI) approach.  
• Use the narrow information window surrounding each FOMC statement (t = 0) to sweep out slow-moving fundamentals.  
• The continuous treatment is the surprise component of the policy action (ΔiSurprise = announced Δi – ΔiExpected from futures). Because the futures contract settles on the average effective funds rate for the current month, the price recorded at t – 1 reflects the market’s expectation before news is released. Any residual is therefore (quasi-)random to agents up to t.  
• Estimate the causal effect by regressing abnormal stock-market returns in a 1-day (or intraday) window on ΔiSurprise across events.  
Why appropriate:  
– Timing (minutes) of the announcement is known; markets cannot react earlier.  
– Fed funds futures provide a market-based counterfactual of what would have happened absent new information.  
– The window is so small that confounding macro forces are plausibly constant.

-----------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
-----------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable: Surprise change in the target federal funds rate (bps).  
Treated “observation”: each FOMC announcement-day return, weighted by the continuous surprise.  
Control (counterfactual): The same equity return had the surprise been zero, proxied by the regression intercept; operationally we also include (i) announcement days with zero surprises and (ii) non-announcement days for placebo tests.

Timing: Day t is the calendar day of the statement (3:00 pm ET). Using close-to-close returns aligns the announcement with that day’s return. Alternative intraday robustness uses 30-minute window bracketing the statement.

Variation: Cross-section over 131 events and, for heterogeneity tests, across 17 industries and ~6,000 individual firms.

-----------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
-----------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Exogeneity of ΔiSurprise: Given publicly available information up to t – 1, the residual between actual and expected policy is unpredictable.  
  Plausible: Fed decision-making is secret; futures incorporate public expectations.

A2. No other systematic news in the same narrow window that is correlated with ΔiSurprise.  
  Plausible but check: occasional macro releases (CPI, GDP) on the same day are scheduled at 8:30 am; Fed statements are 2:15–2:20 pm → non-overlapping.

A3. Stable return-generating process within the window (no time-varying betas across events).  
  Short horizon & market index abnormal-return metric mitigate concern.

A4. Correct measurement of expectations using the front-month federal-funds-futures price.  
  Plausible, but measurement error attenuates results; adjust via contract-length weight (Kuttner adjustment).

-----------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
-----------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Concurrent macro announcements or geopolitical shocks.  
  • Create a “clean” sample: drop dates with major scheduled releases after 1 pm or unexpected shocks (e.g., 9/11).  
  • Add controls: dummy for any same-day macro release.

T2. Measurement error in ΔiExpected (futures).  
  • Use Kuttner’s convexity-adjusted futures surprise.  
  • Instrument with rate changes implied by Eurodollar futures as robustness.

T3. Anticipatory trading earlier on statement day (leakage).  
  • Replace close-to-close with 30-minute (2:00–2:30 pm ET) intraday returns from TAQ for robustness (if data available).  
  • Placebo test: regress morning-of-announcement returns (open-to-1:00 pm) on ΔiSurprise; coefficient should be ≈ 0.

-----------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
-----------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# Packages
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # robust, clustered regressions
library(lubridate)

# 1. Load data ----------------------------------------------------
crsp <- fread("crsp_daily_returns.csv")          # date, permno, ret, mktvwret
fomc <- fread("fomc_announcements.csv")          # date, d_target, time
futures <- fread("fedfunds_futures.csv")         # date, implied_change_bps

# 2. Construct surprise ------------------------------------------
# merge previous-day futures quote
setkey(fomc, date)
setkey(futures, date)
fomc[, exp_change := futures[.SD, implied_change_bps, roll = -1]]   # t-1 quote
fomc[, surprise := d_target - exp_change]

# 3. Merge with returns & create event window --------------------
crsp_mkt <- unique(crsp[,.(date, mktvwret)])
data <- merge(crsp_mkt, fomc, by = "date", all.x = TRUE)
data[is.na(surprise), surprise := 0]             # non-announcement days

# 4. Abnormal return (market minus mean non-event) ---------------
mu_non_event <- data[is.na(d_target), mean(mktvwret)]
data[, abret := mktvwret - mu_non_event]

# 5. Main regression ---------------------------------------------
main <- feols(abret ~ surprise, data = data[!is.na(d_target)],
              vcov = ~0)                         # homoskedastic; few events

summary(main)

# Clustered version (across dates) -------------------------------
main_clu <- feols(abret ~ surprise, data = data[!is.na(d_target)],
                  vcov = ~date)
summary(main_clu)

# 6. Robustness: exclude days w/ macro releases ------------------
macro <- fread("macro_release_calendar.csv")     # date, big_release (0/1)
data <- merge(data, macro, by = "date", all.x = TRUE)
robust <- feols(abret ~ surprise, data = data[big_release==0 & !is.na(d_target)],
                vcov = ~date)
summary(robust)

# Robustness 2: placebo (t-1 return) -----------------------------
placebo <- feols(shift(abret, -1) ~ surprise, data = data[!is.na(d_target)],
                 vcov = ~date)
summary(placebo)
```

-----------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
-----------------------------------------------------------------
Theory: Unexpected rate cuts lower discount rates and signal easier future liquidity; equity prices should rise.  
Rule-of-thumb magnitude (based on Campbell-Shiller log-linearization and prior event studies):  
• Market return response ≈ −(0.04 to 0.06) % per 1 bp surprise.  
• Therefore a –25 bp surprise (cut) → +1.0–1.5 % abnormal market return, roughly half of which may reverse over next week if the cut reflects bad news about growth (information effect).

Industry heterogeneity: Higher-duration / interest-sensitive sectors (tech, durable goods) respond ~1.5× market; utilities and energy ~0.5×.

-----------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = satisfied, 0 = weak)
1. Exogenous timing & surprise measure ...................... 1  
2. No simultaneous confounders in ≤ 1-day window ............ 0.8  
3. No anticipatory effects (pre-trend) ........................ 0.9  
4. Correct functional specification / linearity .............. 0.8  
5. Accurate measurement of returns & surprises ............... 0.9  
Total (out of 5) ............................................. 4.4  

Overall, the high-frequency event design combined with market-based expectations provides a compelling quasi-experiment for gauging equity-market reactions to unexpected monetary-policy shocks.
